assets.transcript: Everything starts with a raw ask like 'build me a URL shortener' — ambiguous, and useless as a blueprint until you interrogate it.
First, extract the verbs: what must the system do? Shorten a URL, redirect, count clicks — those are the functional requirements.
Then extract the numbers: ten thousand redirects per second, p99 under fifty milliseconds, four nines — how well it must do it, always numeric.
Those numbers are bounded by immovable constraints — budget, a single region, data-residency law, the size of your team.
Where the functional needs collide with the constraints, you find the driving tradeoff — the one tension this design must resolve.
The architecture is then derived from that tradeoff, not chosen from a catalog — which is why it survives review instead of falling apart.
Someone asks how many servers you need — the answer starts with two product numbers: daily active users and actions per user per day.
Multiply DAU by actions per user and you have total actions per day — the root number every other estimate derives from.
Divide actions per day by 86,400 seconds and you get average requests per second — the mean load on the system.
But traffic is bursty, so multiply the average by a peak factor of two to ten — you provision for the spike, never the mean.
The same actions-per-day number branches to storage: multiply by bytes per record and retention to get storage per year.
Finally, peak RPS times bytes per response gives peak bandwidth — the pipe you must be able to fill at the worst moment.
The chain is crude on purpose: two product numbers place you in an architecture class — one box, one beefy database, or a sharded fleet.
Every request starts at the client, which sends it to the load balancer — the single front door for the whole system.
The load balancer routes to any app server it likes — the servers are stateless, so every instance is interchangeable and one dying costs nothing.
For a read, the app server asks the cache first: a hit returns in microseconds and the request never touches the database at all.
Only on a cache miss do we fall through to the database — the durable source of truth — and the answer refills the cache on the way back.
Anything slow — emails, thumbnails, reports — is not done here; the app just drops a job on the queue and responds to the user immediately.
A worker consumes that job off the critical path, at its own pace — if it is slow or fails, the user's request never feels it.
That is the whole design: one job per box, cache before database, and slow work queued aside so the request path stays fast and hard to kill.
Every request starts at the client and must pass through service A, which is up 99.9 percent of the time — about 8.8 hours of downtime a year.
Service A sits in series with what comes next, and series components multiply availabilities — every dependency you chain drags the total down.
Service B runs as two replicas at 99 percent each; the path fails only if both die at once, so you multiply unavailabilities: 1 percent times 1 percent.
That 0.01 percent joint failure turns two mediocre boxes into 99.99 percent — redundancy buys nearly two extra nines from ordinary hardware.
Now compose the whole path: 99.9 percent times 99.99 percent is about 99.89 — the series chain, not the redundant pair, sets your ceiling.
So four nines is a design property, not a wish: series multiplies you down, parallel multiplies failure away — count the nines along the entire path.
Never pick a database by trend — start from the workload's access pattern, because every store class optimizes a different data model.
First question: does the workload need joins or multi-row transactions? That single answer decides most transactional apps.
If yes, choose relational SQL — Postgres or MySQL give you joins, secondary indexes, and ACID; bolting joins into app code loses consistency.
If not, ask whether every read is a point lookup by a known key — sessions, caches, simple lookups fit this shape.
When the key is always known, key-value stores like Redis or DynamoDB give O(1) gets and easy partitioning — but no query beyond the key.
Otherwise ask if the data is a nested aggregate read as one unit — if yes, a document store fits; if writes are huge and columnar, go wide-column.
The insight: there is no universally faster database — the skill is matching the store's data model to your access pattern, in this exact order.
A query arrives with a predicate over ten million rows, and the planner's first job is deciding how to find the matches.
The key question is selectivity: what fraction of the table does this predicate actually match?
If the predicate matches many rows, the planner chooses a sequential scan and simply reads every row in order.
If it matches only a few rows, the B-tree wins: an O of log n descent to the leaf, then fetch just the matches.
But the index is never free: every insert and update must maintain the tree, so each index adds a write and storage tax.
So indexes are a precise tool: add them for selective lookups the planner will actually use, and skip them everywhere else.
A user updates their profile: the write goes to the leader, which commits it at log position N and confirms immediately.
The leader streams its replication log to the followers, which apply each change in order and serve the read traffic.
Because replication is asynchronous, one follower is already caught up to N, but the other is still behind — it holds the old profile.
Moments later the same user reads their profile back; hit the lagging follower and they see stale data — their own write vanishes.
The fix is read-your-writes routing: the router remembers the user wrote at position N and only picks a follower that has replayed to N or beyond.
If no follower has reached N yet, the router falls back to the leader — lag never disappears, so you route reads around it, not hope it's zero.
Every record starts with its shard key — we hash that key onto a fixed ring of positions, so placement depends on the key, not on the node count.
From the key's hash position, we walk clockwise around the ring; the first node we hit — here node A — owns that key.
Nodes B and C own the next arcs, so the keyspace is carved into ranges — each node serves only the slice of hashes that lands on its arc.
Now the payoff: adding a node just splits one arc, so only about K over N keys move — modulo sharding would remap nearly the whole dataset.
But the ring can't save a bad key: shard by signup month and every new user hashes to the same few values, melting one node while its peers idle.
So sharding works when two things hold — a high-cardinality, uniform shard key for balance, and consistent hashing to keep rescaling cheap.
Every read starts at the app, which asks the LRU cache for the key first — the database is never the first stop in cache-aside.
If the key is present, that's a hit: the cache returns immediately from memory and the slow database is skipped entirely.
On a miss you pay twice: the cache lookup was wasted, and now the app must load the value from the database anyway.
The loaded value populates the cache, but memory is finite — if the cache is full, LRU evicts the entry untouched the longest to make room.
The cache reports hits and misses as a metric — hit rate is the number that tells you whether the cache is actually earning its keep.
At a 20 percent hit rate, most reads pay cache plus database — a cache only speeds you up when hot data stays resident and the hit rate is high.
A hot key just expired, so 500 concurrent readers all miss the cache in the same instant — this is the makings of a stampede.
Without protection, every one of those misses would hit the database at once; instead, they all funnel into a single-flight guard.
The guard makes the key decision: only the first request through becomes the leader and is allowed to recompute the value.
Everyone else is parked — the other 499 requests simply wait on the leader instead of stampeding the origin themselves.
The leader queries the database exactly once, so the origin sees a single recompute instead of a synchronized flood of 500.
With the fresh value in hand, the leader refills the cache, and every waiter is handed that same shared result.
That's the core insight: collapse N identical misses into one recompute — the herd waits briefly, the origin does the work once.
Every request starts at the client and hits one address: the load balancer, which fronts a pool of identical backends.
The load balancer's first job is spreading work: an algorithm like round-robin or least-connections picks which backend gets each request.
Round-robin gives each backend an equal count of requests, but it is blind to load, so a slow backend quietly piles up work.
Now backend three crashes; without a check, the balancer would keep sending it one request in three and a third of users would see errors.
That is the second job, hiding failures: health checks probe every backend, and backend three stops answering.
After repeated failed probes, the health checker tells the balancer to pull backend three from the pool, so traffic only flows to healthy nodes.
The insight: a load balancer is only as good as its health checks; the algorithm spreads load, but the gated pool is what hides failure.
A user's request never crosses the continent first — it lands at the nearest edge cache, a CDN node sitting in a city close to them.
The edge doesn't guess what's safe to keep — it reads the Cache-Control header, the contract the origin stamps on every response.
Static assets marked public get stored at the edge, so the next user in that city is served in milliseconds and the origin never hears about it.
On a miss, the edge fetches from the origin server once, caches the answer, and every later request for it stays local.
Personalized responses must say no-store — cache someone's account page at the edge and every user in that city sees it.
So private traffic always goes to origin, and the whole system rests on one header: Cache-Control decides what the edge may keep and what it must never touch.
It starts with a network partition: the link between data centers drops, and both sides keep running without seeing each other's writes.
You cannot opt out of partitions — real networks fail. So the partition forces a decision you must have designed in advance.
That decision is CAP's real content: while partitioned, each piece of data gets consistency or availability — never both.
Choose CP and the system stays consistent: it blocks or rejects any request it can't answer correctly, trading uptime for truth.
Choose AP and the system stays available: every request gets an answer, even a stale one, and conflicts are reconciled later.
Money and inventory require CP — a bank serving balances from both sides of a partition is how a customer double-spends.
Feeds and likes require AP — a slightly stale like count is fine, but downtime isn't. The insight: choose C or A per data, not per system.
A payment producer enqueues a charge-card message and returns immediately — the queue decouples it from whoever does the work.
The queue delivers the message to the consumer, but the guarantee is at-least-once: delivered for sure, possibly more than once.
If the consumer finishes the charge but crashes before its ack lands, the queue sees no ack and redelivers — a duplicate arrives.
So before doing anything, the consumer checks a dedup ledger: have I already seen this message id?
If the id is new, the ledger records it and the side effect runs exactly once — the card is charged a single time.
If the id is already recorded, the ledger says skip — redelivery becomes a harmless no-op, which is what idempotent means under at-least-once.
Five copies of your data does not mean fresh reads — what matters is whether the write set and the read set are guaranteed to share a replica.
A write goes out and waits for acknowledgments from W replicas — here it lands on replica 1 and replica 2 before it is confirmed.
Replica 3 never received the write — it still holds the old value, and that is completely normal in a quorum system.
Later, a read fans out to R replicas — it happens to query replica 2 and the stale replica 3.
Because R plus W exceeds N, pigeonhole math forces at least one shared replica — here replica 2 sits in both the write set and the read set.
Replica 2 holds the latest version, so the read compares responses and returns the fresh value — replica 3's stale copy is outvoted.
That is the whole guarantee: choose W and R so the sets must overlap, and every read is certain to touch a replica carrying the newest write.
It starts with a design under review — code that calls a remote service and quietly assumes the network will behave like a local function call.
We run the design through a fallacy audit, checking each of the classic false assumptions engineers carry over from single-machine code.
First flag: the design trusts the network is reliable — there is no timeout and no retry, so one dropped packet leaves threads waiting forever.
Second flag: it assumes latency is zero, making chatty fine-grained calls where every round trip silently adds real milliseconds.
Third flag: hosts are hardcoded, assuming the topology never changes — the moment a server moves or scales, the design breaks.
Each flagged assumption maps to a concrete defense: timeouts and retries for reliability, batching and caching for latency, service discovery for topology.
That is the insight: the fallacies are not trivia — they are an audit checklist where every unstated assumption you catch becomes a specific fix you ship.
Start with the recommendations service — a minor dependency — and it has just gone down.
The product page calls it synchronously and treats it as required, so when recs fails, the product page fails with it.
Failure is transitive: the homepage embeds the product page, so it goes down too — the whole site dies from one small service.
That set of everything knocked out — recs, product page, homepage — is the blast radius: walk the graph from the failure to all its dependents.
The fix is a bulkhead: declare recommendations optional and isolate the failure so it cannot propagate past that edge.
With recs walled off, the bulkhead serves a degraded product page — no recommendations, but the page and homepage stay up.
The insight: blast radius is set by your edges, not your failures — cut the synchronous hard dependency and a tiny outage stays tiny.
The breaker starts CLOSED: every request flows to the dependency, and each failure is quietly counted against a threshold.
When failures cross the threshold, the breaker trips to OPEN — instead of retrying harder, it stops calling entirely and fails fast.
OPEN is the protection: with zero traffic hitting it, the struggling dependency finally gets room to recover instead of a retry storm.
After a cooldown elapses, the breaker moves to HALF-OPEN and lets a single probe request through as a careful test.
That one trial call decides everything: if it succeeds, the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes.
If the trial fails, the breaker re-opens and waits out another cooldown — never flooding a dependency that is still down.
The insight: resilience is not retrying harder — the breaker converts repeated failure into fast failure, so your client stops being the attack.
Start with what you can actually measure: the SLI, a concrete signal of health like the fraction of requests that succeed.
The SLI alone means nothing until you compare it to a target: the SLO, say 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 30 days.
Here is the reframe: one minus the SLO is your error budget, the failure you have explicitly decided to allow, about 43 minutes a month at 99.9.
Every failed request spends that budget, and the burn rate tells you how fast: an afternoon incident can torch a whole month's allowance.
The burn rate is a decision, not a dashboard: burning slow means budget to spare, so ship faster and take risks.
Burning hot means the budget is nearly gone, so freeze risky changes until it recovers; reliability is now a number you spend, not a gut feeling.
Requests arrive at whatever rate clients feel like sending, but your service can only survive a finite rate, so every request first hits the token bucket.
Meanwhile a refill process drips tokens into the bucket at r per second; that steady drip is the sustained rate you are willing to serve long-term.
The bucket holds at most capacity tokens, so a quiet period banks up to b tokens; that stored slack is exactly how big a burst you can absorb at once.
Every request must withdraw one token, so admission reduces to a single question: is there a token in the bucket right now?
If a token is there, the request takes it and gets served; within budget, users never notice the limiter exists.
If the bucket is empty you are past both budgets, so the request is rejected — and under overload you shed low-priority work first to protect what matters.
One bucket encodes two limits: refill rate caps sustained throughput, capacity caps the burst, and shedding turns overload into triage instead of collapse.
Big architecture calls fail when teams trade opinions; this flow replaces debate with a scored, written decision.
Start by enumerating the genuine options on the table, like monolith versus microservices, not just the loudest proposal.
Then define the criteria that matter for this system and weight them: a pre-market-fit startup weights simplicity and velocity, not hyperscale.
Every option is evaluated against every weighted criterion, producing a total score that turns preference into arithmetic you can argue about.
The highest weighted total wins; the lower totals become explicit rejected alternatives instead of silently forgotten paths.
Both outcomes flow into an ADR: record the winner, and just as importantly, record why each alternative lost.
The value is not the arithmetic, it is the forced conversation about weights, plus a written record the next engineer can revisit when constraints change.
A junior starts drawing databases immediately; a senior runs a six-step method that guarantees the diagram answers the actual question.
Step one, frame: clarify functional requirements, non-functional targets, and constraints, because everything downstream is derived from these answers.
Then estimate: back-of-envelope math on peak requests per second, storage, and bandwidth, so the design is sized to reality instead of taste.
Only now do you sketch the high-level design: the major components and the request path, at whiteboard altitude, not implementation detail.
Then deep-dive into the pieces that matter most for this problem, like the data model and storage choices, using the requirements you framed.
Next, hunt the bottleneck: with your estimates in hand, ask which component breaks first at the stated scale, that risk is where the design earns its keep.
Finish by naming the tradeoffs you made and what you would revisit; the method, not the diagram, is what separates senior from junior.
One client, two request paths: writing a new short link, and the read-heavy redirect that serves every click after it.
Creates hit the rate limiter first, so a burst of write traffic can never starve the system or mint codes faster than it can store them.
Admitted creates take a monotonic id, encode it in base sixty-two, and store the mapping — each id is used once, so uniqueness holds by construction.
The mapping lands in a store sharded by short code with consistent hashing, so writes and storage spread across nodes as the system grows.
Redirects are the hot path: the client hits the cache, and on a hit we answer straight away with a 301 to the long URL.
On a miss, the cache falls back to the owning shard, fills itself, and still resolves — slower, but never wrong, because the store is the source of truth.
The design is the composition: limiter, id generator, shards, and cache each solve one problem, and the invariants — unique codes, correct redirects — hold across all of them.
Everything starts with the spec: traffic numbers, data types, budget, and availability targets — plus the design you built to meet them.
First, the capacity gate: your back-of-envelope peak RPS and storage must fit the provisioned budget — servers times per-server capacity.
Pass capacity and the consistency gate takes over: every data type must land in a store whose guarantees match its correctness needs.
Next, the cache gate: your hit-rate math must show the read-heavy load actually stays off the backing stores at peak.
Then containment: when a shard or dependency fails, the blast radius must stay bounded — the design survives partial failure by arithmetic, not hope.
Notice the gates are chained with AND — one failed check anywhere invalidates the whole design; there is no partial credit.
Only when all four computed checks pass does the design earn its verdict — that's the course's founding principle: proof, not vibes.
